alt: Three kinds of liability. Personal: the defendant answers for their own negligence. Vicarious, in outline: an employer is liable for an employee’s tort where the relationship is employment or akin to it (Various Claimants) and the tort is closely connected with the job (Lister; Mohamud). Joint: two or more defendants causing the same damage are each liable for the whole, with contribution under the 1978 Act.
caption: One wrongdoer, an employer standing behind one, or several sharing the same damage.

alt: Duty starts with the neighbour principle in Donoghue v Stevenson (Bourhill v Young: not a foreseeable victim). Following Robinson, an established category is simply applied; a genuinely new duty is tested by Caparo’s three stages: foreseeability, proximity, and fair, just and reasonable. Policy at stage three includes floodgates, defensive practices (Hill) and combat (Mulcahy).
caption: Established categories apply directly; Caparo is for genuinely new duties.

alt: A table of the objective standard for each class of defendant: children (Mullin v Richards), learners (Nettleship v Weston), amateurs (Wells v Cooper), experts (Philips v William Whiteley) and professionals (Bolam, Bolitho, Roe v Minister of Health).
caption: Same objective test, but the reasonable person is matched to the defendant’s class.

alt: Factual causation by the but for test, with multiple causes (Wilsher; Bonnington Castings) and the Fairchild exception. Then intervening acts that break the chain: a third party (Knightley v Johns), the claimant (McKew v Holland) or a natural event. Finally remoteness: the kind of damage must be foreseeable (Wagon Mound), though not the manner (Hughes); a different kind is too remote (Doughty); the thin skull rule applies (Smith v Leech Brain).
caption: But for, then no intervening act, then a foreseeable kind of damage.

alt: The general rule bars pure economic loss (Spartan Steel; Murphy). The exception is negligent misstatement under Hedley Byrne v Heller, which needs special skill, knowledge that the claimant will rely, and reasonable reliance. Caparo found no duty to investors generally; Chaudhry v Prabhakar and Smith v Eric S Bush found a duty.
caption: Economic loss is recoverable mainly through a special relationship of reliance.

alt: Primary victims, within the range of physical injury, recover for psychiatric illness (Page v Smith). Secondary victims must pass the three Alcock controls: a close tie, proximity in time and space including the immediate aftermath (McLoughlin v O’Brian), and their own unaided senses; the Law Commission would keep only the close tie. White and Paul show rescuers and relatives in medical cases get no special treatment.
caption: Primary victims need foreseeable physical danger; secondary victims face three controls.

alt: The Kai scenario in four steps: an established duty to occupants (Robinson); breach judged as a competent electrician, with a minority practice possibly satisfying Bolam and Bolitho; but for causation and a foreseeable kind of harm; and Lucy as a secondary victim likely to satisfy Alcock, comparable to McLoughlin.
caption: Duty, breach, causation and remoteness in order; then each Alcock control for Lucy.
